query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build chamber during selective laser melting (SLM) of high-entropy alloy components will reduce thermal gradients during solidification, thereby reducing fabrication‐induced defects, improving dimensional precision, and enhancing mechanical integrity relative to a standard room-temperature build.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA parts produced via SLM at ambient chamber temperatures, which typically exhibit high cooling rates, residual stresses, layer mismatches, and microstructural inhomogeneities leading to defects such as porosity and microcracks.
generation.intervention: Introduce an elevated build chamber preheating step (for example, maintaining the chamber at an optimized temperature in the range of 200–300°C) throughout the SLM process.
generation.conditions: This intervention is applicable for additively manufactured high-entropy alloys (using either elemental powder mixtures or pre-alloyed powders) intended for high-performance structural applications (e.g., aerospace or reactor components) where complex geometries and superior mechanical properties are critical. The chamber preheating should be implemented during the entire build process.
generation.structural_mediator: The elevated chamber temperature reduces the thermal gradient between the melt pool and the surrounding material, leading to slower cooling rates. This in turn promotes more uniform layer fusion, minimizes residual stress accumulation, and results in a homogeneous microstructure with reduced porosity and fewer microcracks.
generation.mechanism: By preheating the build chamber, the cooling rate during solidification is reduced. This moderates the thermal contraction, limiting warping and residual stresses, and enhances the metallurgical bonding between layers. Such homogenization of the microstructure reduces the likelihood of defect nucleation and results in more precise dimensions and improved mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline SLM process at room temperature, the preheated samples are expected to show significantly improved dimensional accuracy (i.e., reduced warping and layer misalignment), lower defect density (reduced porosity and microcracking), and enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., higher tensile strength, improved ductility).
generation.baseline: Standard SLM-produced HEA components fabricated at ambient build chamber temperature, which often suffer from rapid cooling-induced residual stresses, elevated defect density, and dimensional inaccuracies.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated for HEAs processed via SLM that are sensitive to thermal gradients; however, if the preheating temperature is set too high, it may lead to excessive grain coarsening or undesired phase transformations. The optimal preheating range may also vary with the specific HEA composition and machine characteristics.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal preheating temperature and the quantitative degree of improvement in dimensional precision and mechanical properties remain uncertain and will likely depend on the specific alloy composition, powder characteristics, and SLM system. The effect may vary for alloys with extreme melting points or thermal conductivities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of a high-entropy alloy using SLM: one with a standard (ambient temperature) chamber and one with an elevated chamber preheating regime (e.g., 250°C). Maintain all other processing parameters identical. After fabrication, conduct a comparative analysis of the dimensional accuracy, defect content (via microscopy and porosity measurements), and mechanical properties (through tensile and fatigue tests).
measurements: Dimensional accuracy (e.g., measurement of warpage and layer uniformity)
Defect analysis (e.g., porosity percentage, microcrack density via optical/electron microscopy)
Mechanical testing (e.g., yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility, and fatigue life)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision, reduced defect density, or enhanced mechanical performance compared to the non-preheated batch, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 depicts the surface morphology of 16 groups of single passes of the AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy laser cladding orthogonal experiment. It can be observed that the macroscopic quality of the cladding is satisfactory, the surface roughness is minimal, and there are no discernible defects such as cracks, folds, and so forth. The cross-sectional morphology is depicted in Figure 5, demonstrating that the fusion cladding layer renders a strong metallurgical link with the substrate, and no defects such as cracks and peeling are observed. The orthogonal experimental scheme and cross-sectional measurement results are shown in Table 4. From the data in Table 4, it can be seen that during the laser cladding process of AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, the mechanism by which process parameters affect the cladding effect is very complex, and no obvious change law can be found from the data alone.

The study was subject to a few limitations, the foremost of which was the absence of pre-alloyed powder of the desired chemical composition. Thus, mechanical alloyed powder was used instead, which had a few drawbacks of its own. Only small powder quantities with comparatively coarse particle sizes could be established. Therefore, a small PBF-LB machinery able to cope with these conditions was employed, but it lacked the ability to preheat the fabrication chamber. Despite these difficulties, however, the CrFeNiTi MPEA was successfully processed by means of PBF-LB, and samples with large defect-free sections were produced. This serves as a good indicator that this type of alloy is suitable for the PBF-LB process, and with better processing circumstances, significantly larger, defect-free samples should be attainable.
